newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo industry to grow 10 pct, exports 39 pct - IZIT.
newsitem.headline: Yugo industry to grow 10 pct, exports 39 pct - IZIT.

text.p: Yugoslavia should record industrial growth of 10 percent and export expansion of just under 39 percent this year but its cash-starved economy will not meet official targets, the respected IZIT Market Research Institute said on Friday.
Government forecasts are for a 13 percent jump in Gross Domestic Product (GDP), 14 percent rise in industry output and 48 percent surge in exports.
But IZIT economist Tomislav Milisavljevic said: "We can expect a modest growth, weaker than expected but slightly better than in 1996."

Industry grew by 7.9 percent and exports by 39 percent in the first five months of this year. This compared to total 7.1 percent industry and 5.8 percent GDP growth in 1996. No exports growth figures for 1996 are available as Yugoslavia emerged from U.N. sanctions only late in November 1995.

"The economy needs investment for growth, but apart from the Telekom money Yugoslavia cannot count on another major investment by the end of 1997, because it will not meet all conditions to return to world financial institutions," he said.
Milisavljevic referred to almost $1 billion raised from a sale of 49 percent stake of Telekom Srbija to Italian and Greek firms, the sole recepient of which is the Serbian Development Fund.

The government should keep the fund free from any political influence in allocating funds promised for upgrading infrastructure, kick-starting factories and funding export-oriented industries, Milisavljevic added.

He cautioned against directing the Telekom money into servicing state debt to pensioners and public sector workers and consumption because such a move would prompt the central bank to intervene with its depleted forex reserves to no real effect.
Meanwhile, the business climate in May and early June was seen deteriorating due to low consumer demand and overall lack of competitiveness.
Almost 62 percent of Yugoslav companies exported at prices below their production costs, while 50 percent could not meet international quality standards, an IZIT survey showed.
IZIT insisted tight money policy, stable dinar and prices were the only bright spots in the economy over the past five months.

Although total income of the impoverished population rose 12.6 percent in real terms from January to May over the same period 1996, average income remained low, frequently close to subsistance level, Milisavljevic said. State gross revenues during the period reached 15.987 billion dinars ($2.81 billion) and were 3.8 percent higher in real terms than in the same period 1996.
But while budget revenues rose 10.8 percent in real terms, pension and health fund income fell 5.3 percent in real terms.
Investment in industrial fixed assets dropped 47 percent while investment in fixed assets of state organisations rose 53 percent, he added. ($1 = 5.6892 Yugoslav dinars)
